{{Short description|Study of spaces with group actions}}
{{More citations needed|date=April 2018}}

In [[mathematics]], '''equivariant topology''' is the study of [[topological space]]s that possess certain symmetries. In studying topological spaces, one often considers [[continuous function (topology)|continuous maps]] <math>f: X \to Y</math>, and while equivariant topology also considers such maps, there is the additional constraint that each map "respects symmetry" in both its [[domain of a function|domain]] and [[codomain|target]] spaces.

The notion of symmetry is usually captured by considering a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> on <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> and requiring that <math>f</math> is [[Equivariant map|equivariant]] under this action, so that <math>f(g\cdot x) = g \cdot f(x)</math> for all <math>x \in X</math>, a property usually denoted by <math>f: X \to_{G} Y</math>. Heuristically speaking, standard [[topology]] views two spaces as equivalent "up to deformation," while equivariant topology considers spaces equivalent up to deformation so long as it pays attention to any symmetry possessed by both spaces. A famous theorem of equivariant topology is the [[Borsuk–Ulam theorem]], which asserts that every <math>\mathbf{Z}_2</math>-equivariant map <math>f: S^n \to \mathbb R^n</math> necessarily vanishes.

== Induced ''G''-bundles ==
An important construction used in [[equivariant cohomology]] and other applications includes a naturally occurring group bundle (see [[principal bundle]] for details).

Let us first consider the case where <math>G</math> acts [[Group_action#Remarkable properties of actions|freely]] on <math>X</math>. Then, given a <math>G</math>-equivariant map <math>f:X \to_G Y</math>, we obtain sections <math>s_f: X/G \to (X \times Y)/G </math> given by <math>[x] \mapsto [x,f(x)]</math>, where <math>X \times Y</math> gets the diagonal action <math>g(x,y)=(gx,gy)</math>, and the bundle is <math>p: (X \times Y)/G \to X/G</math>, with fiber <math>Y</math> and projection given by <math>p([x,y])=[x]</math>.  Often, the total space is written <math>X \times_G Y</math>.

More generally, the assignment <math>s_f</math> actually does not map to <math>(X \times Y)/G</math> generally. Since <math>f</math> is equivariant, if <math>g \in G_x</math> (the [[isotropy]] subgroup), then by equivariance, we have that <math>g \cdot f(x)=f(g \cdot x)=f(x)</math>, so in fact <math>f</math> will map to the collection of <math>\{[x,y] \in (X \times Y)/G \mid G_x \subset G_y\}</math>. In this case, one can replace the bundle by a [[Equivariant cohomology#Homotopy quotient|homotopy quotient]] where <math>G</math> acts freely and is bundle homotopic to the induced bundle on <math>X</math> by <math>f</math>.

== Applications to discrete geometry ==
In the same way that one can deduce the [[ham sandwich theorem]] from the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem, one can find many applications of equivariant topology to problems of [[discrete geometry]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Using the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: Lectures on Topological Methods in Combinatorics and Geometry|title-link= Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem|first=Jiří|last=Matoušek|authorlink=Jiří Matoušek (mathematician)|series=Universitext|publisher=Springer|year=2003}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Discrete and Computational Geometry, Second Edition|date=2004-04-15|publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC|isbn=9781584883012|editor-last=Goodman|editor-first=Jacob E.|edition= 2nd|location=Boca Raton|language=English|editor-last2=O'Rourke|editor-first2=Joseph}}</ref> This is accomplished by using the configuration-space test-map paradigm:

Given a geometric problem <math>P</math>,  we define the ''configuration space'', <math>X</math>, which parametrizes all associated  solutions to the problem (such as points, lines, or arcs.) Additionally, we consider a ''test space'' <math>Z \subset V</math> and a map <math>f:X \to V</math> where <math>p \in X</math> is a solution to a problem if and only if <math>f(p) \in Z</math>. Finally, it is usual to consider natural symmetries in a discrete problem by some group <math>G</math> that acts on <math>X</math> and <math>V</math> so that <math>f</math> is equivariant under these actions. The problem  is solved if we can show the nonexistence of an equivariant map <math>f: X \to V \setminus Z</math>.

Obstructions to the existence of such maps are often formulated [[abstract algebra|algebraically]] from the topological data of <math>X</math> and <math>V \setminus Z</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/matschke/thesisMatschke.pdf|title=Equivariant topology methods In discrete geometry|last=Matschke|first=Benjamin}}</ref> An archetypal example of such an obstruction can be derived having <math>V</math> a [[vector space]] and <math>Z = \{0\}</math>. In this case, a nonvanishing map would also induce a nonvanishing section <math>s_f:x \mapsto [x,f(x)]</math> from the discussion above, so <math>\omega_n(X \times_G Y)</math>, the top [[Stiefel–Whitney class]] would need to vanish.

== Examples ==
* The identity map <math>i:X \to X</math> will always be equivariant. 
* If we let <math>\mathbf{Z}_2</math> act antipodally on the [[unit circle]], then <math>z \mapsto z^3</math> is equivariant, since it is an [[Even and odd functions|odd function]].
* Any map <math>h:X \to X/G</math> is equivariant when <math>G</math> acts trivially on the quotient, since <math>h(g\cdot x)=h(x)</math> for all <math>x</math>.
